25749: 'Peace'; the Gospels do not give her name, which comes from Josephus
25754: Royal princess; later wife of Philip the tetrarch and then of Aristobulus of Chalcis
25755: Dances at Herod's birthday and asks for John's head
25756: Her dance pleases Herod Antipas, who rashly promises her anything. After asking her mother what to request, she asks for John the Baptist's head on a platter, and receives it.
25757: The Gospels call her only 'the daughter of Herodias' and describe her as a young girl. The Jewish historian Josephus names Herodias's daughter as Salome and says she later married her great-uncle Philip the tetrarch, and after his death her cousin Aristobulus. She is a different person from Salome the follower of Jesus.
25758: Mark 6:22 says the daughter of Herodias danced and pleased Herod and his guests; Mark 6:24 says she went out and asked her mother what to request. Mark 6:22 and 6:28 call her korasion, 'girl'. Some manuscripts of Mark 6:22 read 'his daughter Herodias', which creates a textual puzzle.
25759: Josephus, *Antiquities* 18.5.4, gives her name and marriages. Coins from her later marriage to Aristobulus show her portrait. The famous 'Dance of the Seven Veils' comes from Oscar Wilde's 1891 play, not the Bible.
25760: The text puts the blame mainly on Herodias, with the girl acting as her mother's instrument and Herod as the weak ruler who fears losing face.
25762: Medieval and modern art often turned her into a seductive figure; the Gospels say nothing about seduction and call her a girl.
25763: Young, eager to please, turning to her mother for the answer.
25767: Philip, tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis
25768: If Herod the Great died in 1 BC
25769: Tetrarch (ruler of a quarter) of the lands north-east of Galilee
25771: Ruler in the fifteenth year of Tiberius
25772: Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry partly by naming Philip as tetrarch of Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis.
25774: He rebuilt the town of Paneas at the springs of the Jordan and renamed it Caesarea in honour of the emperor; it became known as Caesarea Philippi, where Peter later confessed Jesus as the Messiah.
25775: Philip was a son of Herod the Great who ruled the mostly non-Jewish lands north-east of the Sea of Galilee from 4 BC until his death in AD 34. Josephus remembers him as a mild and fair ruler. He rebuilt Paneas as Caesarea Philippi and enlarged Bethsaida, renaming it Julias. He married Salome, the daughter of Herodias.
25776: Luke 3:1 names him as tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis. The Gospels mention the city he named, Caesarea Philippi (Matt 16:13).
25777: Josephus, *Antiquities* 18.4.6, records his death in the twentieth year of Tiberius after ruling 37 years. Mark 6:17 calls Herodias's first husband 'Philip'; most historians think this was a different son of Herod (called Herod by Josephus), not the tetrarch, though some think Mark refers to the tetrarch (debated).
25778: Measured and administrative, more interested in building towns and minting coins than in religious quarrels.
25781: Ethnarch (ruler of a people) of Judea, Samaria and Idumea
25782: Joseph avoids Judea because of him
25783: After Herod the Great dies, Joseph hears that Archelaus is ruling Judea in his father's place and is afraid to go there; warned in a dream, he settles the family in Nazareth in Galilee.
25785: After complaints from both Jews and Samaritans about his brutality, the emperor Augustus removes him and banishes him to Vienne in Gaul. Judea then comes under direct Roman rule through governors (later including Pontius Pilate).
25786: Archelaus was a son of Herod the Great and a Samaritan wife, Malthace, and full brother of Herod Antipas. When Herod died in 4 BC, Augustus gave Archelaus the central part of the kingdom (Judea, Samaria and Idumea) with the lesser title of ethnarch. His rule was so harsh that in AD 6 Rome removed him and made Judea a Roman province. His date of death is unknown.
25787: Matthew 2:22 is his only mention by name: Joseph 'heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod' and was afraid.
25788: Josephus (*Antiquities* 17.9.3 and 17.13.2) describes him massacring about 3,000 people at the Temple at the start of his reign and his later banishment. When he went to Rome to have his rule confirmed, a delegation of his subjects went after him to protest.
25790: Many scholars think Jesus' parable of a nobleman who goes to a far country to receive a kingdom while his citizens send a delegation saying 'we do not want this man to reign over us' (Luke 19:12-27) echoes Archelaus's trip to Rome. Others see only a general resemblance to how client kings were appointed.
25791: Insecure and heavy-handed, quick to answer opposition with force.
25793: 'Augustus' means 'revered' or 'majestic', a title given by the Senate in 27 BC
25796: Sole power after the Battle of Actium
25799: Becomes sole ruler of the Roman world
25800: He defeats Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the naval Battle of Actium, ending Rome's civil wars. In 27 BC the Senate gives him the title Augustus.
25801: Decree that all the world should be registered
25802: Luke says a decree of Augustus for a registration (census) is why Joseph and Mary travel from Nazareth to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born. The date and nature of this census are debated (see Quirinius).
25804: After Herod the Great's death he divides the kingdom among Herod's sons Archelaus, Antipas and Philip, and in AD 6 removes Archelaus.
25805: Augustus was the first Roman emperor. He ended a century of civil war and ruled from 27 BC to AD 14, a period remembered as the start of the Pax Romana ('Roman peace'). Jesus was born during his reign. Luke names him to set the birth of Jesus on the stage of world history: the most powerful man on earth issues a decree, and it brings a poor couple to Bethlehem.
25806: Luke 2:1 says a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. He is not named elsewhere in the Bible, though Acts 25:21 uses the title 'Augustus' (Sebastos) for a later emperor.
25807: Augustus was honoured in inscriptions as a 'saviour' who brought peace, and the birthday of Augustus was called 'good news' (euangelia) in the Priene calendar inscription of 9 BC. He was officially 'son of the divine' after the deification of Julius Caesar. His own account of his achievements survives as the *Res Gestae Divi Augusti*.
25808: Many scholars read Luke 2 as a quiet contrast: the angels announce good news, a Saviour, and peace on earth (Luke 2:10-14) using the same vocabulary the empire used for Augustus.
25809: No surviving Roman source mentions a single empire-wide census under Augustus, though he did order many provincial censuses. Some think Luke compresses several of these; others think he refers to a registration in Herod's kingdom (debated).
25810: Calm, cautious and formal, a master of image who speaks of restoring order and the old Roman virtues.
25814: Emperor during Jesus' ministry and crucifixion
25817: Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, usually reckoned as AD 28/29 (or AD 26/27 if counted from a shared rule with Augustus).
25819: Asked whether paying tax to Caesar is lawful, Jesus asks for a denarius, points to Caesar's image on it, and says to give Caesar what is Caesar's and God what is God's. The coin was most likely a denarius of Tiberius.
25821: The crowd warns Pilate, 'If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend,' and the chief priests declare, 'We have no king but Caesar.'
25822: Tiberius was the stepson and adopted heir of Augustus and ruled the Roman Empire from AD 14 to 37. He is the 'Caesar' of the Gospels during Jesus' adult life: Jesus' ministry, crucifixion and resurrection all happened in his reign. The Roman historian Tacitus also dates Jesus' execution under Pontius Pilate to the reign of Tiberius. The city of Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee, built by Herod Antipas, was named after him.
25823: Luke 3:1 names him directly. The Gospels refer to the reigning emperor simply as 'Caesar' (Matt 22:17-21; Luke 23:2; John 19:12). John 6:23 mentions the city of Tiberias.
25824: Tacitus, *Annals* 15.44, says Christ 'suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of the procurator Pontius Pilate' (paraphrased). In his later years Tiberius withdrew to the island of Capri, leaving government largely to the praetorian prefect Sejanus until Sejanus's fall in AD 31.
25826: Some read Jesus' answer as accepting a legitimate role for government; others stress the second half, that people bear God's image and belong wholly to God, so Caesar's claim is limited. Both readings are widely held.
25827: Gloomy, suspicious and dry; a reluctant ruler who distrusted flattery.
25831: Roman senator, general and provincial governor
25832: The census 'when Quirinius was governor of Syria'
25833: Luke ties the registration that brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem to the time when Quirinius governed Syria.
25835: When Judea became a Roman province in AD 6, Quirinius carried out a census for tax purposes. It sparked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean, which Gamaliel mentions in Acts.
25836: Quirinius was a Roman senator and general who served as governor of Syria (which oversaw Judea) and ran a well-known census of Judea in AD 6, according to Josephus. Luke links Jesus' birth to a census under Quirinius. That creates a well-known puzzle, because Matthew and Luke both place Jesus' birth while Herod the Great was alive, and Herod died around 4 BC, about ten years before Quirinius's Judean census.
25837: Luke 2:2 says 'this was the first registration when Quirinius was governing Syria'. Acts 5:37 mentions the revolt of Judas the Galilean 'in the days of the census'.
25838: Josephus, *Antiquities* 18.1.1, describes Quirinius's census of Judea after Archelaus was deposed. Tacitus, *Annals* 3.48, records his death in AD 21.
25840: Many critical scholars think Luke confused the dates and linked Jesus' birth to the famous AD 6 census.
25842: Some scholars translate Luke 2:2 as 'this registration happened before Quirinius governed Syria', which removes the conflict; critics reply that this is a strained reading of the Greek.
25844: Others argue that Quirinius held an earlier command in the region before 4 BC, or that an earlier census began under Herod and was completed under Quirinius; critics say the evidence for an earlier governorship is thin.
25845: Efficient, ambitious and bureaucratic; he speaks in lists and deadlines.
25847: The text does not give the man's name; 'Legion' is the name the spirits give, after a Roman army unit of about 5,000 soldiers
25851: Decapolis (largely Gentile region east of the Sea of Galilee)
25853: Proclaimer of Jesus in the Decapolis
25856: Living among the tombs, breaking every chain, crying out and cutting himself, he runs to Jesus. Asked his name, he answers 'Legion, for we are many.'
25858: Jesus allows the spirits to enter a herd of about two thousand pigs, which rush into the lake and drown. The townspeople find the man clothed and in his right mind, and in fear they ask Jesus to leave.
25860: He begs to go with Jesus, but Jesus sends him home to tell what the Lord has done. He proclaims it throughout the Decapolis, and everyone marvels.
25861:
This unnamed man lived among the tombs on the eastern, mostly Gentile, side of the Sea of Galilee, tormented by many evil spirits. When Jesus asked his name, the spirits answered 'Legion'. Jesus freed him, and the spirits went into a herd of pigs that rushed into the lake. Instead of letting him join the disciples, Jesus sent him home, and he became the first person to tell Gentile towns about Jesus.

Mark and Luke speak of one man; Matthew speaks of two. The place is given differently in manuscripts and Gospels as the country of the Gerasenes, Gadarenes or Gergesenes.
25862: Mark 5:3-5 describes his strength, isolation and self-harm. Mark 5:9 gives the name Legion. Mark 5:15 describes him sitting, clothed and in his right mind. Matthew 8:28 has two men in the country of the Gadarenes.
25864: Many Christians read the story as a literal deliverance from demonic powers, showing Jesus' authority over evil even in Gentile territory.
25866: Some scholars note the military word 'Legion' and the pigs (the boar was an emblem of a Roman legion stationed in the region) and read the story as also hinting at Roman occupation. Others think this reads too much into it.
25868: Matthew's two men may include a second, less prominent sufferer; Mark and Luke focus on the one who spoke and later preached.
25869: Once wild and broken, now calm, grateful and eager to tell anyone who will listen.
25871: The text does not give his name; a centurion commanded about 80 to 100 Roman soldiers
25873: Roman officer in charge of the crucifixion
25877: Seeing how Jesus died, he says, 'Truly this man was the Son of God' (Mark and Matthew), or 'Certainly this man was innocent' (Luke).
25879: Pilate summons him to confirm that Jesus is already dead before releasing the body to Joseph of Arimathea.
25880: The unnamed centurion supervised Jesus' crucifixion. When Jesus died, he declared him the Son of God (in Mark and Matthew) or innocent (in Luke). In Mark, he is the first human being to call Jesus 'Son of God' after the death on the cross, and he was a Gentile and an executioner.
25881: Mark 15:39 says he stood facing Jesus and saw how he breathed his last. Matthew 27:54 says he and those with him saw the earthquake and were terrified. Luke 23:47 says he praised God. Mark 15:44-45 has him report Jesus' death to Pilate.
25883: Many see his words as a full confession of faith that forms the climax of Mark's Gospel (compare Mark 1:1).
25885: The Greek can also be read 'a son of God', which a pagan soldier might have meant in a more limited sense; scholars debate how much he understood, though Mark clearly intends readers to hear the full meaning.
25886: Later tradition named him Longinus and often merged him with the unnamed soldier who pierced Jesus' side with a spear (John 19:34). Tradition says he became a Christian and a martyr. The Gospels give no name.
25887: Acts of Pilate (Gospel of Nicodemus), later recensions; Western martyrologies
25888: Hardened and matter-of-fact, then suddenly awed, speaking with a soldier's bluntness.
25895: Called from the tax booth; hosts a feast
25896: Jesus sees Levi at his tax booth and says 'Follow me'; he leaves everything and follows. He then holds a great feast for Jesus with many tax collectors and sinners, and Jesus answers critics: 'I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.'
25897: Levi is the name Mark and Luke give to the tax collector whom Jesus called from his booth at Capernaum. Matthew's Gospel tells the same story but calls the man Matthew, and lists 'Matthew the tax collector' among the Twelve. So most readers, ancient and modern, take Levi and Matthew to be one person with two names. This is a short cross-reference profile; see Matthew for the full story.
25898: Mark 2:14 calls him 'Levi the son of Alphaeus'. Luke 5:27-29 calls him Levi and says he made a great feast. Matthew 9:9 tells the same call of 'a man named Matthew', and Matthew 10:3 lists 'Matthew the tax collector' among the apostles. No list of the Twelve includes a Levi.
25900: Most identify Levi with Matthew: the stories are nearly identical, and Jews of the time often had two names (compare Simon/Peter, Saul/Paul). 'Matthew' may have been a new name given by Jesus or a second name.
25902: A few, ancient and modern, distinguish them. Clement of Alexandria quotes the second-century teacher Heracleon listing Matthew and Levi separately. Some modern scholars think Matthew's Gospel deliberately put the apostle's name into Mark's story.
25904: Because Levi is 'son of Alphaeus' and an apostle is 'James son of Alphaeus' (Mark 3:18), some suggest they were brothers; Alphaeus was a common name and the Gospels never say so.
25905: Shrewd with money and used to scorn, now generous and glad to throw open his house.
25911: 'Can anything good come out of Nazareth?'
25912: Philip tells him they have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael scoffs, but comes. Jesus calls him 'an Israelite in whom there is no deceit' and says he saw him under the fig tree. Nathanael confesses, 'You are the Son of God, the King of Israel,' and Jesus promises he will see greater things.
25913: At the lakeside appearance of the risen Jesus
25914: He is among the seven disciples fishing on the Sea of Galilee when the risen Jesus appears and provides a large catch.
25915: Nathanael appears only in John's Gospel, as one of the first people Jesus called and later as one of the disciples who saw the risen Jesus by the Sea of Galilee. John says he came from Cana. He is traditionally identified with Bartholomew, one of the Twelve, but the Bible never makes that link directly. This is a short cross-reference profile; see Bartholomew for the apostle's wider story.
25916: John 1:45-49 tells his call and confession. John 21:2 calls him 'Nathanael of Cana in Galilee'. He does not appear in the lists of the Twelve, which name Bartholomew instead (Matt 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14; Acts 1:13).
25918: In the first three Gospels Bartholomew is listed right after Philip, and in John it is Philip who brings Nathanael. 'Bartholomew' is a family name meaning 'son of Tolmai', so the man may also have had a personal name, Nathanael. John never mentions Bartholomew, and the other Gospels never mention Nathanael. This identification became common in the medieval church.
25919: Not one of the Twelve (minority view)
25920: Some, including Augustine in his sermons on John, thought Nathanael was not one of the Twelve at all; John uses the word 'disciples' more broadly than 'the Twelve'.
25921: Frank and a little skeptical, with a dry wit, but quick to give his whole heart once convinced.
25922: Lazarus (in the parable of the rich man)
25928: A poor man covered with sores lies at a rich man's gate, longing for scraps, while dogs lick his sores. Both die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's side; the rich man is in torment in Hades. Abraham says a great gulf is fixed between them and refuses to send Lazarus to warn the rich man's brothers, because 'if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.'
25929: Lazarus is the poor beggar in a story Jesus told in Luke 16. He is the only character in any of Jesus' parables who is given a personal name. His name means 'God has helped', fitting a man helped by no one on earth. He is a different person from Lazarus of Bethany, whom Jesus raised from the dead in John 11.
25930: Luke 16:20-21 describes him lying at the gate, covered with sores. Luke 16:22 says he died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side ('bosom'). Luke 16:25 contrasts what each man received in life. He never speaks in the story.
25932: Most interpreters read it as a parable teaching about wealth, compassion and the sufficiency of Scripture. Some, noting the personal name and the absence of 'a parable' label, argue Jesus was describing real people.
25933: What it teaches about the afterlife (debated)
25934: Some take its picture of Hades and 'Abraham's bosom' as real information about the state after death; others think Jesus used familiar Jewish imagery to make a moral point, so details should not be pressed. See /afterlife.
25936: Some readers note the ending, about someone rising from the dead and still not being believed, and connect it with the raising of Lazarus in John 11, after which leaders plotted against Jesus. This link is suggestive but not stated.
25937: Medieval tradition called the rich man 'Dives' (Latin for 'rich man'), and Lazarus became the patron of lepers; hospitals for lepers were called 'lazar houses'.
25938: Latin Vulgate wording of Luke 16:19; medieval European usage
25939: Silent in the story; if he spoke, he would speak softly, without bitterness, as one who has finally been comforted.
25941: The text does not give his name; the title combines details from three Gospels
25945: Wealthy seeker who declined Jesus' call
25946: Man of great wealth; a 'ruler' (possibly a synagogue or local leader)
25947: 'What must I do to inherit eternal life?'
25948: He runs up, kneels, and asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. He says he has kept the commandments since his youth. Jesus, looking at him, loves him, and tells him to sell what he has, give to the poor, and follow. He goes away sorrowful, for he has great possessions.
25949: This unnamed man came to Jesus asking how to gain eternal life. He had kept the commandments, and Mark says Jesus looked at him and loved him. But when Jesus told him to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow him, he went away sad. The common name 'rich young ruler' combines details: all three Gospels say he was rich, only Matthew says he was young, and only Luke calls him a ruler.
25950: Mark 10:21 says Jesus loved him. Matthew 19:20 calls him a young man; Luke 18:18 calls him a ruler. All three record Jesus' saying that it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God (Mark 10:25).
25952: Some Christians (for example many in the monastic and Anabaptist traditions) see the command to sell everything as a real call to voluntary poverty for those who would follow Jesus fully.
25954: Others read it as a command aimed at this man's particular attachment to wealth, showing that whatever rules a person's heart must be surrendered, rather than a rule for every believer.
25956: Some Protestant readers see Jesus exposing the limits of law-keeping, since the man could not do the one thing asked; the disciples' question 'Who then can be saved?' is answered: 'with God all things are possible' (Mark 10:27).
25957: Earnest, polite and sincere, used to doing things right, and visibly torn.
25958: The widow of Nain and her son
25959: The text names neither mother nor son
25960: Son of the widow of Nain
25962: Young man raised from the dead
25965: Jesus meets a funeral procession for the only son of a widow. Moved with compassion, he tells her 'Do not weep', touches the bier, and says 'Young man, I say to you, arise.' The dead man sits up and begins to speak, and Jesus gives him back to his mother. The crowd says, 'A great prophet has arisen among us; God has visited his people.'
25966: At the gate of the village of Nain in Galilee, Jesus met the funeral of a young man, the only son of a widow. Without being asked, he raised him to life and 'gave him to his mother'. Luke alone tells the story. For a widow in that society, losing her only son could mean losing her means of support, so the miracle restored both of them.
